title: The Financial Bubble Cycles Are Getting Worse
summary: The financialization of our economy, now penetrating Silicon Valley, is generating storms that are both more frequent and more destructive.

By


Zachary D. Carter


Mr. Carter is the author of “The Price of Peace: Money, Democracy and the Life of John Maynard Keynes.”


Nov. 16, 2026


It wasn’t too long ago that Silicon Valley was celebrating the greatest invention in economic history. A dazzling new medium called cryptocurrency had arrived — at once an extraordinary investment, a government-proof digital money and perhaps a way[to bring world peace](https://www.cnbc.com/2021/07/21/jack-dorsey-hopes-bitcoin-will-help-bring-about-world-peace.html) . It would end global poverty and cure inflation. The possibilities were endless — until the public face of the crypto revolution landed in federal prison and the American president began winning his family millions through Trump-branded crypto schemes.


Cryptocurrency still exists, though few take seriously the grandiose promises of yesteryear. As the public’s enthusiasm for digital currency faded, some of its most prominent boosters began showering praise on another shiny object: The artificial intelligence universe is just lousy with crypto players. A.I. “is our alchemy, our Philosopher’s Stone — we are literally making sand think,” trumpeted Marc Andreessen, whose firm has been one of the most influential crypto and A.I. players over the past decade.


Of course, the extreme prognostications about artificial intelligence aren’t *exactly* like the woo-woo crypto hype of 2020. A.I. already has some genuinely useful applications in software development. It might even blow up the world! Maybe that’s why Silicon Valley’s hype machine has been so successful at turning the economy into a massive one-way bet on delivering a still undefined type of “superintelligence” to the globe. Last year,[according to](https://www.stlouisfed.org/on-the-economy/2026/jan/tracking-ai-contribution-gdp-growth) the St. Louis Fed, nearly 40 percent of American economic growth came from the A.I. build-out.


These days, however, excitement is mutating into anxiety. A major A.I.-themed hedge fund collapsed over the summer. Days ago, shares of the A.I. chip giant Nvidia plummeted upon the abrupt resignation of its megawatt chief executive amid allegations of extramarital affairs with a Chinese spy and two women who reported to him. Whatever technological changes may lie in store, the bigger picture is starting to look a lot like a movie we’ve seen before — wild promises and warnings, unusual financing arrangements and the collapse of highflying adventurers. One of our newest industries is following a highly familiar script: The A.I. build-out has become so dependent on the riskiest lending practices of Wall Street that Silicon Valley itself might now be better understood as a wild, unregulated division of the banking sector.


If you haven’t seen this movie, it usually ends in a mess: the 2008 financial crisis, or the collapse of railway mania in 1840s Britain that spurred an industrial depression, or the Panic of 1873 that caused a global catastrophe so bad they called it the Great Depression until that other one came along.


When financial history repeats, fatalism can be hard to resist. It is genuinely disheartening to see people pitch and fall for farcical nonsense, time after time. But our present is not simply repeating the recent past — in important ways, the cycle is getting worse.
